newsitem.title: FINLAND: Russia spells out what it wants from summit.
newsitem.headline: Russia spells out what it wants from summit.

text.p: Russia made clear there was no way it would step back from its opposition to NATO on the eve of its Helsinki summit with the United States, but also left open a path for progress on a range of other issues.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky lifted the lid slightly on furious behind-the-scenes negotiations with the closest Russia has come to a summit "wish list".
"In recognising NATO as a very important partner for us, we are trying to minimise the possible damage for Russian-U.S. Russian-West relations if NATO expands eastwards," he said.
"There's a very intense negotiating process which has reached the stage of discussion of concrete proposals for a document which could be signed," he said.
"We would like such a document to appear, be signed, to have a binding nature for both sides, Russia and NATO."

"I won't plunge into too much detail because it is part of concrete and for the moment secret diplomacy but I will just say that we consider for the following key elements to be included in the document," he said.
It should lay down general principles for relations between Russia and NATO. "No one has a right to a veto but no one has the right to spring surprises," he said, by way of an example.
There should be a concrete outline of steps towards transforming NATO into a more political organisation.
A new institution or mechanism independent of NATO to govern Russian-NATO relations should be set up.
"Not 16 plus one but a full 17," he said, referring to the 16 existing members of the alliance.
The document should contain NATO obligations to take into account Russia's concerns about expansion.
"Not moving nuclear weapons, or large military units and there's also talk, negotiations about military infrastructure," he said.
"Verbal reassurances that nuclear forces won't enter the territory of new members are not enough. We need judicial, written obligations that it won't happen."

Yastrzhembsky said the important thing was for such document to be acceptable, and that if agreement was not reached by the July, when NATO plans to invite in some former Warsaw Pact members, consultations could continue.
He also made clear, in a message clearly aimed at Russia's nationalist opposition, that negotiations did not mean Russia was softening its approach.
"The consultations which are going on do not mean and will not mean our agreement to expansion," he said.
Sticking to the tough tone he used to tell the West that NATO expansion would be a big mistake, Yastrzhembsky said Russia hoped for a boost in investment from the United States.
"Great attention will undoubtedly be paid to U.S.-Russian relations, especially in the economic sphere," he said.

"We would like the good words, the wonderful declarations which have come out of Washington recently regarding Clinton administration's intention to strengthen relations with Russia..to be fulfilled with concrete plans and projects.

Above all in such areas as direct investment by...American firms in the Russian economy and a very important change for us would be U.S. support for Russia's plans to join the biggest international institutions, the World Trade Organisation or the transformation of the Group of Seven into a full Eight."
